item.content:encoded:
Translator from the Korean branch. Can someone please restate the underlined words?

The Revolution in 1979 changed little for the organization as such; the less diehard-fundamentalist Muslims began pretending outwardly to be so in order to match new political realities, but nobody in the new government is quite willing to tamper with ORIA's traditional autonomy so long as ORIA makes no attempt to influence the Revolution. Which it doesn't; some members of the organization have left-wing, atheistic, or anti-Ayatollah tendencies, but all of the organization is strongly loyal to their homelands — Iran in particular, but also other Mideastern nations, local tribes, clans, or families — and the group is mostly apolitical in nature.

From the ORIA Hub,

Sentient memetic organisms developed throughout the Muslim world around the conception of "djinn" as developed by the new Muslim ruling class.

The "djinn" identified by ORIA may not necessarily be the djinn spoken of the Quran, but a term for these unknown alien beings. It is within possibility that "djinn" was a term coined due to similarities with whatever the audience at that time can fathom.

Perhaps the modern-day ORIA is trying to get their members out of the usage of "djinn" and emphasise them as memetic beings or creatures otherwise definable by science (as opposed to the superstitious connotations of "djinn").

That's fair; while there are a fair number of articles based on creatures featured in religious texts, the accuracy with which they are depicted varies pretty wildly. I can't speak for the members of the team who made the hub, but I would imagine that the shift in the role and nature was based on something more substantial than (just) "we want ghostmans."

If I recall correctly, one of the Foundation RPs, Tamlin House, was set inside of a djinn container the size of a large city. Perhaps that has something to do with it? Not that it has much to do with the underlying issue, but it's still interesting and semi-relevant, in my opinion.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It's not that I'm super offended or anything, it's just that isn't what the jinn are. At all.

What we know about the Jinn is that they are a race of unseen beings made from smokeless fire. They do not primarily interact in our seen world, though occasionally there can be contact between them and human beings, many times with those who involve themselves in idolatrous practices. Like humankind, they have been given free choice, and the message of Islam was sent to them also. Shayton (Iblees), for example, is from amongst the Jinn, as are other devils. Some cultures have come to build up more fear and superstition around the jinn than is realistic; jinn rarely reach out to interact with normal people. Thus, people should not try to interact with them either, steering clear of doubtful matters involving them. This is the advice of my shaykh.

http://seekershub.org/ans-blog/2011/07/31/the-jinn-the-reality-of-their-existence-and-how-to-protect-ourselves-from-them/

Simply put, the jinn aren't spooky magical ghosts we can hang around with freely, let alone recruit into our fictitious Middle Eastern eldritch monster agencies. I'm not sure if writing about the jinn constitutes as something sinful (though as a writer I prefer to avoid that kind of stuff completely) but as a Muslim it kills immersion for me completely.

item.content:encoded: Thanks, oops, not exactly but i did run some of the details past some of those experts in question and referenced the Internet a lot, thanks and yes, the djinn are specifically designed to add a faerie-ish, Seelie Court-esq urban fantasy underground political whatever to the ORIA universe, and yes, very much a secular/religious organization. Basically, my idea for ORIA is that the core or nucleus was founded very Horizon Initiative-style, where people of different origins, cultures, and religions came together for a shared goal (i.e. protecting the Middle East and other predominantly Muslim regions from outside interference and colonization, as well as to manage the fairly fragile human/Djinn alliance). The Ayatollahs tolerate its less-than-orthodox nature because a) ORIA serves too useful a purpose in keeping Iran stable in the world of the paranormal and anomalous, and b) ORIA is still a fairly secret organization and its members are very clearly instructed to remain apolitical and try to moderate their views publicly.
